hook.line: Some Spanish words only exist in the plural, or change meaning when they go plural. If you say "un celo" for one jealousy, nobody knows what you mean.

examples.en: They put the handcuffs on him.

examples.es: Los restos del edificio estaban en la calle.
examples.en: The remains of the building were in the street.

examples.es: El resto de la gente se fue.
examples.en: The rest of the people left.

rule:
Three words change when they go plural.

*los celos* = jealousy. It only works in the plural, and you *have* it: *tener celos de*. English says "be jealous of", Spanish says "have jealousies of".

*el resto* = the rest. *Los restos* = what is left after something is destroyed or someone dies: remains.

*la esposa* = wife, but *las esposas* also means handcuffs. Context tells you which: *le pusieron las esposas*.

In short, do not translate these word for word. Learn them as a plural unit.
smallPrint: Teachers call these nouns with a plural of special meaning, or *pluralia tantum* when no singular exists, as with *celos*.

options: He has a lot of brothers.
He's jealous of his brother.
He misses his brother.
They found archaeological remains.
They rested in the museum.
They found the rest of the group.
They put the wives on him.
They gave him a wife.
They put the handcuffs on him.
I'm jealous of your coffee.
I love your coffee.
I need your coffee.

readAndPick.es: Los restos del edificio estaban en la calle.
options: The rest of the building was inside.
The remains of the building were in the street.
The building rested in the street.

readAndPick.es: El resto de la gente se fue.
options: The rest of the people left.
The remains of the people left.
The people rested.

readAndPick.es: Mi esposa tiene celos de mi socio.
options: My wife is jealous of my partner.
My wife is the partner's friend.
My wife has handcuffs.

readAndPick.es: La policía llegó con las esposas.
options: The police arrived with their wives.
The police arrived with the handcuffs.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick the right word and type the whole sentence: *Tiene ___ de su hermano.* (celos or celo)
Type in Spanish: They found archaeological remains.
yourTurn.why: *Restos* in the plural means what is left of something.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: They put the handcuffs on him.
yourTurn.why: *Las esposas* in this context means handcuffs.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: I'm jealous of your coffee. (to a friend)
Type in Spanish: The rest of the people left.
yourTurn.answer: El resto de la gente se fue.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it about the building: *Encontraron restos arqueológicos.* Say: The remains of the building were in the street.
yourTurn.answer: Los restos del edificio estaban en la calle.
yourTurn.why: *Los restos* with *del* tells you whose remains.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: My wife is jealous of my partner.
yourTurn.answer: Mi esposa tiene celos de mi socio.
yourTurn.why: Wife is singular *esposa*; the jealousy is *tiene celos*.

pitfalls.why: Almost. *Estar celoso* exists too, but the everyday way is *tener celos*.

pitfalls.wrong: Tiene un celo de su hermano.
pitfalls.why: Almost. In this meaning, *celos* never goes singular.

pitfalls.wrong: El resto del edificio estaban en la calle.
pitfalls.right: Los restos del edificio estaban en la calle.
pitfalls.why: Almost. *El resto* is just "the rest"; the leftover pieces are *los restos*.

personal: Tell me about a time you had *celos*, or who you would put *las esposas* on in a story.
